help.intro: When a pronoun is the object of the verb it changes form, just as in English (I → me, he → him): Ich sehe dich, du siehst mich, wir kennen ihn. Five of the nine change completely — ich → mich, du → dich, er → ihn, wir → uns, ihr → euch — and four stay exactly as they were: sie (her), sie (them), es and Sie. The one that catches English speakers is 'it': a thing is er, sie or es by its gender, so 'I see it' is Ich sehe ihn for der Tisch, sie for die Lampe, es for das Buch. Choose the pronoun by the noun's gender, then put it in the accusative — which, for a der-word, means ihn.
help.tips[0].title: Five change, four stay
help.tips[0].text: ich → mich · du → dich · er → ihn · wir → uns · ihr → euch. sie, es and Sie keep their form in the accusative.
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: Do you love me? – Yes, I love you.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: Are you visiting us? – Yes, I am visiting you on Sunday.
help.tips[0].check.q: Kommst du mit? Ich brauche ____. (you, one friend)
help.tips[0].check.why: As the object of brauchen, du becomes dich — one of the five pronouns that change.
help.tips[1].title: 'it' is ihn, sie or es
help.tips[1].text: A thing keeps its gender as a pronoun. der Schlüssel → Ich habe ihn. die Tasche → Ich habe sie. das Buch → Ich habe es.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: Where is the key? – I have it.
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: Where is the bag? – I don't see it.
help.tips[1].trap: 'it' is three words in German. Reaching for es every time is the most common beginner's pronoun error.
help.tips[1].check.q: Wo ist der Kuli? – Ich habe ____.
help.tips[1].check.why: Kuli is a der-noun, so 'it' is er — and as an object er becomes ihn.
help.tips[1].visual.caption: 'it' copies the gender of the noun it stands for.
help.tips[1].visual.rows[0].label: the noun
help.tips[1].visual.rows[1].label: it
help.tips[2].text: In the accusative sie is her *and* them, and Sie (capital) is the formal you. Context decides, exactly as in the nominative.
help.tips[2].examples[0].en: I know her / them. – I know you.
help.tips[2].examples[1].en: Where's Anna? I can't see her.
help.tips[2].check.q: In „Herr Braun, ich verstehe Sie nicht.“, who is Sie?
help.tips[2].check.why: A capital Sie in the middle of a sentence is the formal 'you' — here Herr Braun. Small sie would be her or them.
help.tips[3].text: Say the five changers as one chant: mich, dich, ihn — uns, euch. If the pronoun is sie, es or Sie, nothing changes.
help.tips[3].examples[0].en: He sees us. We see you (all).
help.tips[3].examples[1].en: I know her/them. I know it. I know you (formal).
help.tips[3].check.why: wir changes to uns as an object: mich, dich, ihn — uns, euch.
help.remember[0]: mich, dich, ihn, uns, euch — five change; sie, es and Sie stay the same.
help.remember[1]: A thing is he/she/it by its article: der → ihn, die → sie, das → es.
help.context.en: Have you seen my key? – Yes, I have it. It's in my bag. – And my glasses? – I've got those too, I'll bring them to you. – Thanks! I love you. – I know. And I need the car – do you have it?
help.mistakes[0].why: er is only for the subject; as an object it is ihn.
help.mistakes[2].why: du becomes dich as an object.
help.hook: Say 'I see him', 'she loves us' and 'do you have it?' in German — object pronouns are just a handful of small words.
help.table.caption: Subject and object pronouns
sentences[0].english: That's me in the photo. Do you see me?
sentences[0].why: The one being seen is the object: ich becomes mich in the accusative.
sentences[1].english: You are my best friend. I like you a lot.
sentences[1].why: mögen takes an accusative object: du becomes dich.
sentences[2].english: That is Tom. I know him.
sentences[2].why: er becomes ihn as the object — the only pronoun pair where the accusative really changes shape.
sentences[3].english: That is Anna. I know her.
sentences[3].why: sie ('she') stays sie in the accusative — it never changes.
sentences[4].sentence: Das ist das Buch. Ich lese ____. (it)
sentences[4].english: That is the book. I read it.
sentences[4].why: es stays es in the accusative — like English 'it'.
sentences[5].english: We are at home. Are you visiting us?
sentences[5].why: wir becomes uns as the object — 'us'.
sentences[6].english: You are my friends. I visit you on Sunday.
sentences[6].why: ihr becomes euch as the object — 'you all' being visited.
sentences[7].english: Those are my friends. I'm meeting them.
sentences[7].why: sie ('they') stays sie in the accusative.
sentences[8].sentence: Ich verstehe ____ gut, Frau Müller. (you, formal)
sentences[8].english: I understand you well, Mrs Müller. (formal)
sentences[8].why: Formal Sie stays Sie in the accusative — always with its capital S.
sentences[9].english: Do you hear me? I'm talking to you!
sentences[9].why: hören takes an accusative object: ich → mich.
sentences[10].sentence: Ich rufe ____ heute Abend an. (you, informal)
sentences[10].why: anrufen takes the accusative — German 'calls you', du → dich (not 'to you').
sentences[11].sentence: Wo ist der Schlüssel? Ich finde ____ nicht. (it — der Schlüssel)
sentences[11].english: Where is the key? I can't find it.
sentences[11].why: der Schlüssel is a der-word, so 'it' is er — and as the object, ihn.
sentences[12].sentence: Die Musik ist toll. Ich höre ____ gern. (it — die Musik)
sentences[12].english: The music is great. I like listening to it.
sentences[12].why: die Musik is a die-word, so 'it' is sie — the pronoun follows the noun's gender.
sentences[13].sentence: Das Fenster ist offen. Bitte mach ____ zu. (it — das Fenster)
sentences[13].english: The window is open. Please close it.
sentences[13].why: das Fenster is a das-word: es — the only gender where 'it' really is es.
sentences[14].english: We're going to the cinema. The film interests us.
sentences[14].why: interessieren takes the accusative: wir → uns — the film interests us.
sentences[15].sentence: Die Jacke ist super! Ich nehme ____. (it — die Jacke)
sentences[15].english: The jacket is great! I'll take it.
sentences[15].why: die Jacke is a die-word: 'it' is sie, unchanged in the accusative.
sentences[16].sentence: Mein Kaffee ist kalt. Ich trinke ____ nicht. (it — der Kaffee)
sentences[16].english: My coffee is cold. I'm not drinking it.
sentences[16].why: der Kaffee is a der-word: 'it' is er, and as the object it turns into ihn.
sentences[17].sentence: Kinder, ich liebe ____! Aber jetzt ist Schlafenszeit. (you, plural)
sentences[17].english: Children, I love you! But now it's bedtime. (you all)
sentences[17].why: ihr → euch as the object of lieben.
sentences[18].sentence: Herr Schmidt, ich höre ____ nicht gut. Bitte sprechen Sie lauter. (you, formal)
sentences[18].english: Mr Schmidt, I can't hear you well. Please speak louder. (formal)
sentences[18].why: Formal Sie keeps its form in the accusative: Sie, capital S.
